title: Seizure Classification and Antiseizure Therapy: Treat the Seizure Type, Patient, and Cause
bottomLine: Antiseizure treatment follows seizure type/epilepsy syndrome, recurrence risk, comorbidity, pregnancy potential and drug toxicity—not the fact that one convulsion occurred. First stabilize ongoing seizure, identify provoked causes, classify the event, then choose long-term therapy only when recurrence risk and diagnosis justify it.
recognize: Focal seizures may have preserved or impaired awareness and can evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic activity; generalized epilepsies have different drug implications.
Hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbance, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal, toxins, infection and acute brain injury can provoke seizures without establishing chronic epilepsy.
differentiate: Syncope may include brief jerks but often has a perfusion trigger and rapid recovery; prolonged postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury and stereotyped events favour seizure but no single sign is diagnostic.
Psychogenic nonepileptic events require respectful diagnostic confirmation and do not justify dismissing future episodes.
assessment: Obtain witness description/video when available, onset/focal features, duration, post-event state, prior subtle events, medications/substances, sleep, pregnancy potential, neurologic symptoms and family history.
Assess injury, airway, glucose and ongoing status first in an acute event.
workup: Use glucose/electrolytes and cause-directed testing acutely; EEG and MRI are selected for unprovoked or focal events according to the first-seizure pathway.
Urgent imaging is driven by focal deficit, trauma, anticoagulation, cancer/immunocompromise, fever or persistent altered state rather than ordered automatically for every recurrent known seizure.
management: Treat ongoing convulsive status through the emergency benzodiazepine-based pathway and escalate rapidly.
Correct provoked causes before deciding on chronic medication.

Select long-term antiseizure therapy by seizure type, reproductive risk, renal/hepatic function, psychiatric/cognitive effects, interactions and adherence; neurology input is appropriate when classification is uncertain.
medicationSafety: Valproate carries major reproductive/teratogenic risk and should not be a casual default in people who could become pregnant.
Do not abruptly stop chronic antiseizure medication because withdrawal can provoke seizures; drug-specific CBC, liver, renal, sodium or serum-level monitoring is used when clinically indicated.
redFlags: New first seizure in an older adult with focal features
counselling: Discuss driving restrictions/reporting according to province/territory, bathing/swimming/heights safety, adherence, alcohol/sleep triggers and pregnancy planning.
followUp: Review recurrence, adverse effects, adherence, diagnostic data and whether the original epilepsy classification still fits.
examTrap: Starting indefinite antiseizure therapy after a clearly provoked single seizure without correcting the cause or estimating recurrence risk.
oneLinePearl: Classify the seizure and cause before you classify the patient as needing lifelong medication.

title: Stroke: Reperfuse What You Can, Then Prevent the Next Event
bottomLine: A new focal neurologic deficit is stroke until proven otherwise. Establish last-known-well, check glucose, activate a stroke-capable emergency pathway, obtain urgent brain and vascular imaging, and let time/imaging determine reperfusion candidacy; after stabilization, secondary prevention is mechanism-specific rather than one universal antiplatelet plan.
recognize: Sudden unilateral weakness/numbness, facial droop, aphasia/dysarthria, visual-field loss, neglect, ataxia or posterior-circulation symptoms can be stroke.
A normal early CT excludes many hemorrhages but does not prove there is no ischemic stroke.
differentiate: Hypoglycemia, seizure/postictal deficit, migraine aura and functional symptoms can mimic stroke, but evaluation should not be delayed when the syndrome is plausible.
Ischemic stroke, intracranial hemorrhage and cerebral venous/other vascular disease require different acute treatment.
assessment: Document exact onset/last-known-well, baseline function, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use and last dose, recent surgery/bleeding, BP, glucose and neurologic deficit while maintaining ABCs.
Do not allow a prolonged office workup to delay EMS transfer.
workup: Use urgent noncontrast brain imaging plus vascular imaging through the regional stroke pathway; laboratory testing should not create avoidable reperfusion delay.
After the acute phase, assess rhythm/AF, carotid/vascular disease, lipids, BP, diabetes and other etiologic clues.
management: Activate emergency stroke care; stroke specialists determine IV thrombolysis and endovascular thrombectomy eligibility from time, imaging and contraindications.
After hemorrhage is excluded, antithrombotic strategy is selected by stroke mechanism and bleeding risk.
Secondary prevention includes mechanism-appropriate antiplatelet or anticoagulation, BP/lipid/diabetes/smoking management, rehabilitation and selected carotid/cardiac interventions.
medicationSafety: Do not give antiplatelet therapy before hemorrhage is excluded in a new acute stroke presentation.
Anticoagulant use/timing materially affects reperfusion decisions and later secondary-prevention timing; provide exact medication history to the stroke team.
counselling: Teach FAST/other stroke warning signs, medication adherence and that recurrence prevention depends on the identified mechanism.
followUp: Close the loop on vascular imaging, rhythm monitoring, rehabilitation, antithrombotic plan and risk-factor targets after discharge.
examTrap: Waiting for outpatient MRI or a second office assessment when a patient has a new disabling focal deficit in a reperfusion time window.
oneLinePearl: Acute stroke is a time-and-imaging emergency; prevention afterward is a mechanism problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices — Acute Stroke Management and Secondary Prevention
Heart & Stroke Canadian Stroke Best Practices

title: TIA: Resolved Symptoms Are a Warning, Not Reassurance
bottomLine: Transient focal neurologic symptoms can precede disabling stroke. Determine whether the event was truly focal/vascular, identify the highest-risk timing and features, obtain rapid brain/vascular/cardiac evaluation, and start mechanism-appropriate secondary prevention after hemorrhage and competing diagnoses are addressed.
recognize: Transient unilateral weakness/numbness, aphasia/dysarthria or monocular/visual-field loss are classic focal symptoms.
Motor or speech symptoms and events occurring recently carry high early recurrence concern.
differentiate: Migraine aura, seizure, hypoglycemia, syncope and peripheral vestibular disease can mimic TIA; positive spreading sensory phenomena and stereotyped recurrent episodes may point away from ischemia but require judgment.
A nonfocal spell of generalized weakness or isolated presyncope is not automatically a TIA.
assessment: Clarify onset, maximal deficit, duration, focality, vascular risk, AF/palpitations, carotid disease, medications and bleeding history.
Perform a full neurologic/vascular assessment even if symptoms have resolved.
workup: Use urgent brain and vascular imaging and ECG/rhythm assessment through the local TIA/minor-stroke pathway; additional cardiac testing depends on suspected source.
Do not use a risk score as the sole reason to delay imaging/referral when the clinical event is high risk.
management: Highest-risk recent TIA/minor stroke needs same-day stroke-capable assessment rather than a routine distant neurology referral.

Start antiplatelet therapy after hemorrhage is excluded when appropriate; short-term dual-antiplatelet therapy is reserved for selected high-risk TIA/minor ischemic stroke without high bleeding risk under current stroke guidance.
AF/cardioembolic disease changes the prevention strategy to anticoagulation when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not combine antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy routinely without a specific indication because bleeding risk rises.
Carotid or intracranial disease may require urgent specialist intervention beyond medication alone.
counselling: Explain that symptom resolution does not remove early stroke risk and teach immediate return for any recurrent focal deficit.
followUp: Ensure all vascular/cardiac results are reviewed and the antithrombotic, BP, lipid and smoking plan is closed-loop.
examTrap: Sending a patient home for routine follow-up because a 20-minute aphasia episode completely resolved.
oneLinePearl: TIA is the warning shot; the workup and prevention clock starts when the symptoms stop.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices — TIA/Minor Stroke and Secondary Prevention

title: Parkinson Disease: Bradykinesia Plus the Pattern, Then Treat Function
bottomLine: Parkinson disease is a clinical syndrome requiring bradykinesia with a compatible parkinsonian pattern and course. Treat the motor and nonmotor problems that impair function, preserve medication timing, integrate rehabilitation, and recognize atypical features that warrant movement-disorder reassessment.
recognize: Bradykinesia with rest tremor and/or rigidity, often asymmetric initially, supports idiopathic Parkinson disease.
Constipation, REM-sleep behaviour disorder, anosmia, depression, orthostatic symptoms and cognitive change can precede or accompany motor disease.
differentiate: Essential tremor is primarily action/postural; antipsychotics/metoclopramide can cause drug-induced parkinsonism.
Early recurrent falls, gaze palsy, severe early autonomic failure, prominent cerebellar signs or poor levodopa response suggest atypical parkinsonism.
assessment: Assess gait/freezing/falls, ADLs, cognition, mood, hallucinations, orthostasis, swallowing, sleep, constipation, impulse-control symptoms and medication timing.
workup: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; imaging is used to evaluate atypical features or alternate diagnoses rather than confirm typical Parkinson disease routinely.
management: Levodopa remains the most effective symptomatic motor therapy; medication selection/timing is individualized to disability, age, adverse effects and patient priorities.
Integrate exercise, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech/swallowing care and falls prevention.
Refer complex motor fluctuations, dyskinesia, atypical signs or advanced-therapy questions to movement-disorder care.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop dopaminergic therapy; severe rigidity/hyperthermia syndromes can follow interruption.
Avoid dopamine-blocking antiemetics/antipsychotics when safer alternatives exist; dopamine agonists can cause impulse-control disorders and sudden sleep attacks.
redFlags: Acute inability to take dopaminergic medication
counselling: Teach exact medication timing, driving/falls/sleep safety and the importance of reporting hallucinations, compulsive behaviours and swallowing problems.
followUp: Track function, motor fluctuations, nonmotor burden, medication adverse effects and caregiver needs over time.
examTrap: Stopping levodopa during hospitalization because the patient is NPO without arranging an alternative dopaminergic plan.
oneLinePearl: In Parkinson disease, medication timing is part of neurologic stability.
sourceBasis: Canadian Guideline for Parkinson Disease, 2nd Edition
Parkinson Canada current healthcare-professional medication resources

title: Essential Tremor: Action Tremor Without Parkinsonian Anchoring
bottomLine: Essential tremor is usually a bilateral action/postural tremor syndrome diagnosed clinically after medication, thyroid, enhanced physiologic and parkinsonian causes are considered. Treat only when disability or distress justifies therapy and match medication/device options to comorbidity and goals.
recognize: Hands/forearms are common, with possible head/voice involvement; tremor is typically most evident with posture or action rather than a classic rest pattern.
Family history is common but not required.
differentiate: Parkinson disease requires bradykinesia and often rest tremor/rigidity; dystonic tremor has abnormal posturing; medication/caffeine/stimulant/thyroid causes can enhance physiologic tremor.
assessment: Ask onset/progression, alcohol/caffeine/stimulants, medications, family history, functional impact and neurologic symptoms.
Examine rest, posture, action, handwriting/spiral, bradykinesia, rigidity, gait and dystonia.
workup: Routine neuroimaging is not required for a classic isolated tremor; test thyroid/metabolic causes or image when history/exam is atypical.
management: If treatment is needed, propranolol or primidone are common evidence-based options when not contraindicated; selected refractory disabling tremor may warrant botulinum toxin, focused ultrasound or deep-brain-stimulation referral.
Address triggering stimulants and occupational adaptations.
medicationSafety: Propranolol can worsen bradycardia, hypotension or bronchospasm; primidone can cause sedation/ataxia and should be titrated carefully, especially in older adults.
counselling: Explain that treatment targets function, not complete tremor elimination, and discuss driving/occupational safety if medication causes sedation.
followUp: Track functional benefit and adverse effects; reconsider diagnosis if new bradykinesia, gait or neurologic findings emerge.
examTrap: Diagnosing Parkinson disease from hand tremor alone without demonstrating bradykinesia or a parkinsonian syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Action tremor points toward essential tremor; bradykinesia changes the diagnosis.

title: Multiple Sclerosis: Establish Disseminated Disease, Then Modify Future Risk
bottomLine: MS diagnosis requires a compatible inflammatory demyelinating syndrome with evidence of dissemination in space/time and exclusion of better mimics. Acute relapse management and long-term disease-modifying therapy are separate decisions; DMT choice/monitoring belongs in neurology and must incorporate infection, pregnancy and treatment-risk context.
recognize: Optic neuritis, partial transverse myelitis, brainstem syndromes, sensory symptoms and focal weakness in younger adults are common presentations.
Heat, fever and infection can temporarily worsen prior deficits without new inflammatory disease.
differentiate: Pseudo-relapse reproduces old symptoms during infection/heat/metabolic stress; stroke, B12 deficiency, NMOSD/MOGAD and structural cord disease can mimic MS.
Nonspecific white-matter lesions on MRI alone do not equal MS.
assessment: Define new vs old deficits, duration, objective findings, infection symptoms, prior episodes, pregnancy plans and current immunotherapy.
workup: MRI brain/spine and CSF/other testing are used through contemporary diagnostic criteria; test specific mimics when the syndrome is atypical.
Before immunosuppressive DMT, screen infections/vaccination/organ function according to the selected agent.
management: Treat functionally significant acute relapse with specialist-guided corticosteroid therapy when appropriate after excluding important infection/pseudo-relapse.
Start/optimize DMT early enough to reduce inflammatory activity, selecting efficacy vs safety from disease activity, comorbidity, pregnancy and patient preference.
Rehabilitation, symptom management and exercise remain important alongside DMT.
medicationSafety: DMTs differ substantially in infection, malignancy, liver/hematologic, vaccination and pregnancy risks; follow current product/specialty monitoring.
Do not abruptly stop certain high-efficacy therapies without a transition plan when rebound inflammatory activity is possible.
counselling: Discuss contraception/pregnancy early, vaccination timing, infection symptoms and why DMT changes future relapse/disability risk rather than immediately reversing established deficits.
followUp: Track relapses, MRI activity, disability, treatment adherence/toxicity and pregnancy/infection plans with MS specialty care.
examTrap: Giving high-dose steroids for every temporary worsening before checking for infection or heat-driven pseudo-relapse.
oneLinePearl: Relapse treats today’s inflammation; DMT changes tomorrow’s risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian MS Working Group treatment-optimization recommendations

title: Peripheral Neuropathy: Map the Pattern Before Ordering the Panel
bottomLine: Neuropathy workup starts with distribution, tempo, fiber type and motor/autonomic involvement. A length-dependent symmetric sensory neuropathy has a different differential from focal mononeuropathy, radiculopathy or rapidly progressive motor weakness; targeted high-yield testing is better than an indiscriminate laboratory panel.
recognize: Diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, CKD, chemotherapy and medications commonly cause length-dependent neuropathy.
Entrapment neuropathy is focal; radiculopathy follows a root pattern; myelopathy produces upper-motor-neuron/cord findings.
differentiate: Burning feet with reduced distal sensation differs from proximal motor weakness, multifocal mononeuropathy and autonomic-predominant disease.
Rapid ascending weakness/areflexia suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome and is not an outpatient neuropathy workup.
assessment: Map sensory modalities, strength, reflexes, gait, autonomic symptoms and foot integrity; review diabetes, alcohol, nutrition, medications/toxins, cancer therapy and family history.
workup: For typical distal symmetric polyneuropathy, use focused testing such as glucose/A1C, B12, CBC/renal/thyroid and serum protein studies when clinically appropriate; electrodiagnostics are most useful when pattern is atypical, motor-predominant, asymmetric or diagnostically uncertain.
Avoid broad low-yield autoimmune/infectious panels without a phenotype that supports them.
management: Treat the cause, protect insensate feet, address falls and use neuropathic-pain therapy when needed.
Urgent neurology/hospital evaluation is required for rapidly progressive weakness, respiratory/autonomic compromise or suspected inflammatory neuropathy.
medicationSafety: Gabapentinoids, TCAs and other neuropathic-pain drugs can cause sedation, falls or anticholinergic effects; adjust for renal function and concurrent opioids/sedatives.
counselling: Teach daily foot/skin inspection when sensation is reduced and realistic goals for neuropathic-pain treatment.
followUp: Track progression/function and revisit the diagnosis if the distribution or tempo changes.
examTrap: Ordering dozens of neuropathy tests before determining whether the process is distal symmetric, focal, radicular, motor or central.
oneLinePearl: Neuropathy workup starts with the map and tempo, not the lab requisition.

title: Dementia: Diagnose the Syndrome, Identify the Cause, Then Discuss Disease-Modifying Eligibility
bottomLine: Dementia diagnosis requires acquired cognitive decline that impairs function after delirium, depression, medications and reversible contributors are assessed. In Canada, selected patients with confirmed early Alzheimer disease may now be candidates for approved anti-amyloid disease-modifying therapy, but eligibility is narrow and requires specialist biomarker, genetic/risk and MRI monitoring—not routine prescribing for undifferentiated dementia.
recognize: Alzheimer disease often begins with progressive episodic-memory impairment; vascular, Lewy-body, frontotemporal and other dementias have different patterns.
Mild cognitive impairment preserves basic functional independence more than dementia but may still qualify as early Alzheimer disease if the required clinical/amyloid criteria are confirmed.
differentiate: Delirium is acute/fluctuating with impaired attention; depression, sleep disorders, hearing/vision loss and medication effects can mimic or worsen cognition.
Normal aging does not cause progressive loss of instrumental function.
assessment: Obtain patient plus collateral history, trajectory, ADLs/IADLs, driving, medications/anticholinergics, mood, sleep, substance use, neurologic symptoms, vascular risk and caregiver strain.
Assess capacity for the specific decision rather than equating a dementia diagnosis with global incapacity.
workup: Use validated cognitive assessment plus focused neurologic/physical exam, basic reversible-cause testing and structural imaging when appropriate.
When anti-amyloid therapy is considered, confirm the specific early-Alzheimer diagnosis and amyloid pathology and complete product/specialist-required APOE/MRI/risk evaluation.
management: Treat reversible contributors and vascular risk, support function/safety/caregivers and use symptomatic cognitive therapy when appropriate.

Health Canada has approved lecanemab and donanemab for selected adults with MCI or mild dementia due to Alzheimer disease with confirmed amyloid pathology and restricted APOE-e4 eligibility; initiation/monitoring is specialist managed.
Advance care planning, driving and medication simplification should be addressed before crisis.
medicationSafety: Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies carry potentially serious amyloid-related imaging abnormality/bleeding risks and require MRI and product-specific monitoring; antithrombotic/bleeding-risk context must be reviewed carefully.
Anticholinergics, sedative-hypnotics and polypharmacy can worsen cognition/falls.
redFlags: New neurologic symptoms during anti-amyloid therapy
counselling: Explain that disease-modifying anti-amyloid therapy is not a cure and is only for a biomarker-confirmed early-Alzheimer subgroup after individualized risk/benefit review.
followUp: Track cognition/function, safety, caregiver burden and treatment adverse effects; reassess diagnosis when the course is atypical.
examTrap: Offering an anti-amyloid drug to any patient labelled 'dementia' without confirming early Alzheimer disease, amyloid pathology and eligibility/safety criteria.
oneLinePearl: Dementia is a syndrome; disease-modifying Alzheimer therapy requires a much narrower confirmed diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Health Canada Drug Product Database/Notices of Compliance — LEQEMBI and KISUNLA
